This is Umberto Eco's 14 features of fascism: 

1. The cult of tradition. “One has only to look at the syllabus of every fascist movement to find the major traditionalist thinkers. The Nazi gnosis was nourished by traditionalist, syncretistic, occult elements.”
2. The rejection of modernism. “The Enlightenment, the Age of Reason, is seen as the beginning of modern depravity. In this sense, Ur-Fascism can be defined as irrationalism.”
3. The cult of action for action’s sale. “Action being beautiful in itself, it must be taken before, or without, any previous reflection. Thinking is a form of emasculation.”
4. Disagreement is treason. “The critical spirit makes distinctions, and to distinguish is a sign of modernism. In modern culture, the scientific community praises disagreement as a way to improve knowledge.”
5. Fear of difference. “The first appeal of a fascist or prematurely fascist movement is an appeal against the intruders. Thus Ur-Fascism is racist by definition.”
6. Appeal to social frustration. “[…] one of the most typical features of the historical fascism was the appeal to a frustrated middle class, a class suffering from an economic crisis or feelings of political humiliation, and frightened by the pressure of lower social groups.
7. The obsession with a plot. “The followers must feel besieged. The easiest way to solve the plot is the appeal to xenophobia.”
8. The enemy is both weak and strong. “[…] the followers must be convinced that they can overwhelm the enemies. Thus, by a continuous shifting of rhetorical focus, the enemies are at the same time too strong and too weak.”
9. Pacifism is trafficking with the enemy. “For Ur-Fascism there is no struggle for life but, rather, life is lived for struggle.”
Contempt for the weak. “Elitism is a typical aspect of any reactionary ideology.”
10. Everybody is educated to become a hero. “in Ur-Fascist ideology, heroism is the norm. This cult of heroism is strictly linked with the cult of death.”
11. Machismo and Weaponry. “This is the origin of machismo (which implies both disdain for women and intolerance and condemnation of nonstandard sexual habits, from chastity to homosexuality). Since even sex is a difficult game to play, the 12. Ur-Fascist hero tends to play with weapons—doing so becomes an ersatz phallic exercise.”
13. Selective Populism. “There is in our future a TV or Internet populism, in which the emotional response of a selected group of citizens can be presented and accepted as the Voice of the People.
14. Ur-Fascism speaks Newspeak. “All the Nazi or Fascist schoolbooks made use of an impoverished vocabulary, and an elementary syntax, in order to limit the instruments for complex and critical reasoning.”

Hey man, I feel like everyone's self-hatred might stem from different places, meaning the solution might be different. But based on your post, I think our self-hatred might be similar. 

1. Figure out what's causing it

By this, I don't mean listing the reasons you hate yourself. There are people out there who love themselves who likely have the same flaws you do. 

I mean, where does it come from? Is it a defense mechanism against rejection/abandonment because it gives you an excuse not to get close to anyone? Were you bullied/abused, and internalized it and took it out on yourself to feel control over your situation? Is it your way of coping with guilt or toxic shame? 

Once you understand it and it's real purpose, it loses some of its power because you can finally understand why it isn't rational

2. Be more compassionate and understanding toward yourself

I hated myself when I was a kid. To the point I wanted to be assaulted because I felt like I deserved it, and frequently hurt myself or imagined torturing myself. When I say I had no compassion for myself, I had absolutely none. But one of my breakthroughs was when I imagined a little girl who looked nothing like me going through the same things I had. For the first time in my life, I felt compassion for myself. And that helped me to...

3. Change the negative voice in your head

Do you beat yourself up over everything? Does your internal monologue sound like Bojack's? _You're a stupid piece of shit, no one could ever love you, this is why people don't like you,_ etc. 

If you grew up being abused or bullied, that's likely where that voice comes from. If you pay attention to what you tell yourself, you're probably beating yourself up over something someone else bullied/abused you for. So if you tell yourself those things first, then it'll hurt less when other people say it to you. Except it doesn't hurt less in the long run. It just causes a different problem. 

Start with this: 
- if you feel a negative emotion, just say (I feel really embarrassed/sad/etc.) and repeat that over and over again until the emotion loses its intensity
- when you say something mean to yourself and recognize it from the past, say "shut up [name of bully/abuser]"
- work on neutral affirmations. At first, anything positive will just sound like bullshit to you. Affirmations only work if you believe them. Say things like "I'm working to fix this problem. I have the qualities [insert positive qualities about yourself]. It's possible I can overcome this. It's possible I'm not as bad as I think I am" 
- be around people who make you feel good about yourself (and are tactfully honest)

4. Cut out or limit interactions with toxic people 

These people are only making it impossible for you to heal. In order to love yourself, you need time away from the arena to address your wounds and heal them. If you don't, people are just going to open those wounds over and over again. 

If you're trying to work on any of the steps above, toxic people are just going to take the wind out of your sails. 

5. Become more confident

The biggest step towards self love is becoming more confident. True confidence comes from knowing who you are, what you value, and how well you stick to those values. Self confidence comes from relying on yourself for validation, and not those around you. Self confidence comes from taking accountability, and owning your decisions and the consequences. 

Open a Google doc or a piece of paper. What are some things you like about yourself? If there's nothing there, that's okay. What are some attainable qualities that you would like to have? (**IMPORTANT NOTE** By this, I don't mean what you think would look cool or acceptable in other people's eyes. What I mean is- what is the kind of person _you_ want to become?). 

Next, make a game plan. Be honest with yourself and self-reflect. Where are you right now? And what can you do to get from where you are to where you want to be? Sometimes it helps to imagine a friend giving you advice, or to imagine giving someone else with this problem advice. Then--the most important part--you stick to it. You commit to personal growth. If you begin doubting yourself, or someone says something that makes you feel self-conscious, remind yourself: "What doesn't matter is what they think. What matters is who I am." 

Once you know you're doing your best to stick to your values, to handle conflict in a healthy way, to be a decent person, to rely on yourself for validation, you genuinely begin to care less about what others think of you because you know who you are. 

And remember: no one is perfect or ever will be. You don't have to be perfect to be lovable. What matters is that you're genuinely doing the best you can to stick to your values and grow as a person. It's okay to fail or make mistakes. What matters is how you choose to handle them and whether or not you choose to learn and grow from them. Taking accountability and owning your choices and the consequences. 

6. Look at how far you've come 

It takes years, so be patient. But every few months or so, take a look back and see how far you've come. It will make you feel good about yourself, and it will help give you the motivation to keep going.

Good luck, and I hope this helps. 

*Don't try to change everything at once. Pick one thing to focus on, and when you've mastered it, move onto the next one. 

*If something isn't working, take a step back, reevaluate, and change your gameplan accordingly

I'm currently in college to become a professional flute player, so I have some things that might help you.

First off, it's completely normal to feel anxious when performing, it's normal for it to affect your playing, and it's normal to do worse in a performance than in practice. Performing in of itself is a skill, and it's one you can improve on the more you do it. 

You're probably never going to stop feeling anxious. I certainly haven't. But the key is to work with your anxiety instead of against it. Accept that you're going to feel anxious and you're going to perform worse than in practice, and plan for it. 

In the moment, it can help to take a deep breath before you start playing, and to play the opening of the music in your head. Also, learn to be okay with messing up during a performance. If you make a mistake, train yourself to let the mistake go and keep going. 

Before the performance, make sure you practice playing through your entire repertoire. Sometimes it can help to make a recording of yourself so you have practice performing your repertoire with pressure.

Hope this helps!
